verses.text: Moreover, brethren, I would not that ye should be ignorant, how that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea;
And were all baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea;
And did all eat the same spiritual meat;
And did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ.
But with many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness.
Now these things were our examples, to the intent we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted.
Neither be ye idolaters, as were some of them; as it is written, The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.
Neither let us commit fornication, as some of them committed, and fell in one day three and twenty thousand.
Neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them also tempted, and were destroyed of serpents.
Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer.
Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come.
Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.

There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.
Wherefore, my dearly beloved, flee from idolatry.
I speak as to wise men; judge ye what I say.
The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
For we being many are one bread, and one body: for we are all partakers of that one bread.
Behold Israel after the flesh: are not they which eat of the sacrifices partakers of the altar?
What say I then? that the idol is any thing, or that which is offered in sacrifice to idols is any thing?
But I say, that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God: and I would not that ye should have fellowship with devils.
Ye cannot drink the cup of the Lord, and the cup of devils: ye cannot be partakers of the Lord’s table, and of the table of devils.
Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? are we stronger than he?
All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but all things edify not.
Let no man seek his own, but every man another’s wealth.
Whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat, asking no question for conscience sake:
For the earth is the Lord’s, and the fulness thereof.
If any of them that believe not bid you to a feast, and ye be disposed to go; whatsoever is set before you, eat, asking no question for conscience sake.
But if any man say unto you, This is offered in sacrifice unto idols, eat not for his sake that shewed it, and for conscience sake: for the earth is the Lord’s, and the fulness thereof:
Conscience, I say, not thine own, but of the other: for why is my liberty judged of another man’s conscience?
For if I by grace be a partaker, why am I evil spoken of for that for which I give thanks?
Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.
Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God:
Even as I please all men in all things, not seeking mine own profit, but the profit of many, that they may be saved.

summary: Paul has just warned that even he could become "a castaway," and he now proves the point from Israel's history. "Moreover, brethren, I would not that ye should be ignorant, how that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea; And were all baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea; And did all eat the same spiritual meat; And did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ." Five times he says "all" — every one of them had the sign, the food, the drink, the Rock — and then the hinge: "But with many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness." The wilderness generation becomes a mirror. "Now these things were our examples, to the intent we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted." Four failures follow in order: idolatry, quoted straight from the golden calf — "The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play"; fornication, where "some of them committed, and fell in one day three and twenty thousand"; tempting Christ, where they "were destroyed of serpents"; and murmuring, where they "were destroyed of the destroyer." All of it "happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come." The application is aimed at Corinthian confidence: "Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall." Yet the warning is immediately cushioned by a promise — "There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it." From this comes the command the whole chapter has been building toward: "Wherefore, my dearly beloved, flee from idolatry." Then, addressing them as adults — "I speak as to wise men; judge ye what I say" — Paul explains why eating at a pagan shrine is not a neutral act. He does it by pointing at their own table: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? For we being many are one bread, and one body: for we are all partakers of that one bread." Israel's worshippers who "eat of the sacrifices" are "partakers of the altar," and the same logic runs the other way: though "the idol is" nothing, "the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God," and Paul will not have them "have fellowship with devils." Hence the flat impossibility: "Ye cannot drink the cup of the Lord, and the cup of devils: ye cannot be partakers of the Lord's table, and of the table of devils. Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? are we stronger than he?" Having closed the shrine, Paul reopens the marketplace. The Corinthian slogan returns with two qualifications — "All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but all things edify not" — followed by the rule that governs the rest: "Let no man seek his own, but every man another's wealth." So: "Whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat, asking no question for conscience sake: For the earth is the Lord's, and the fulness thereof." Accept a pagan's dinner invitation and eat what is served, no questions asked. But if someone points it out — "This is offered in sacrifice unto idols" — then abstain, and Paul is precise about whose scruple governs: "Conscience, I say, not thine own, but of the other." The chapter ends by lifting the whole squabble about menus into doxology and mission: "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God. Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God: Even as I please all men in all things, not seeking mine own profit, but the profit of many, that they may be saved."
takeaways: The fivefold "all" of the opening verses is the argument in miniature. Every Israelite was "under the cloud," "passed through the sea," was "baptized unto Moses," ate "the same spiritual meat" and drank "the same spiritual drink" — and "with many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness." Paul is dismantling a specific Corinthian assumption: that having received the signs guarantees the destination. Sharing in the gifts is not the same as arriving, and the gifts themselves become the measure by which the recipients are judged. What makes the history binding rather than merely instructive is the identification at its centre: "that Rock was Christ." Paul does not say Israel had a shadow while the Church has the substance; he says the same Christ was already feeding and watering them in the desert, which is why he can call their food and drink "spiritual" without irony and still record that they died. If they perished with Christ present among them, no Corinthian can treat presence as immunity, and "let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall" follows with force.

Between the warning and the command Paul plants a promise that keeps the warning from becoming despair: "There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape." Three things are asserted at once — that no Corinthian trial is unprecedented, that the limit on temptation is set by God's faithfulness rather than by our strength, and that the escape is provided along with the trial rather than instead of it. The stated purpose is not the removal of pressure but the capacity "to bear it." And the escape offered in this very chapter is blunt and physical: "flee from idolatry."

Paul answers the question of idol-food not with a theory of matter but with a theology of the table. "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" Eating together at a sacred table joins the eater to what is on it and to everyone else eating — "we being many are one bread, and one body: for we are all partakers of that one bread." That is why Israel's worshippers are "partakers of the altar" and why a shrine banquet cannot be a private matter of digestion. Paul grants that "the idol is" nothing and still forbids the meal, because what stands behind the nothing is not nothing: "the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils."

"Ye cannot drink the cup of the Lord, and the cup of devils" is a statement of impossibility, not merely a prohibition. The Corinthians presumably could and did do both, so Paul is saying the two acts cancel each other — one cannot belong to two tables any more than a spouse can belong to two marriages, which is why he reaches for the language of divine jealousy: "Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? are we stronger than he?" The rhetorical question exposes the real absurdity of their confidence. Enlightened liberty was never strong enough for the contest it had wandered into, and the only sane response to a rival claim on one's allegiance is the one already given: "flee."

Having drawn one hard line, Paul refuses to draw a hundred soft ones. "Whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat, asking no question for conscience sake: For the earth is the Lord's, and the fulness thereof." Meat in the market is God's before it is anyone's, and scrupulous investigation is itself a failure of faith. The single limit is another person: if a man identifies the food as sacrificial, abstain — "not thine own, but of the other" conscience — because the meal has now become a statement he will read. Liberty is real, and it is spent, not hoarded, which is exactly what "Let no man seek his own, but every man another's wealth" means in practice.

The chapter's conclusion refuses to leave the matter at the level of etiquette. "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God" makes the most ordinary act liturgical, and "Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God" names three audiences at once — the synagogue, the pagan neighbour, and the congregation. Paul's own standard is the missionary one he has just described in his own case: "not seeking mine own profit, but the profit of many, that they may be saved." The final measure of a disputed freedom is whether anyone was saved by how it was used.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 17:6 — thou shalt smite the rock, and there shall come water out of it
crossRefs.why: This is the event behind "they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ." The narrative supplies the water and the murmuring at Massah; Paul supplies the identification. Reading them together shows how he handles the wilderness story — not as an illustration borrowed for a sermon, but as an episode in which Christ was already present and already the source of Israel's life.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 32:6 — the people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play
crossRefs.why: Paul quotes this line verbatim as his definition of idolatry, and the choice of quotation is deliberate: he picks not the moment the calf was cast but the moment the people held a feast in front of it. The golden calf was, precisely, a meal at a shrine — which is exactly the practice the Corinthians were defending — and it took place immediately after the covenant had been ratified, by people who had every sign God had given.

crossRefs.label: Numbers 25 — the people did eat, and bowed down to their gods
crossRefs.why: The episode at Baal-peor is Paul's example of fornication, and it fuses the two sins he treats in this letter: Israel joins in the sacrificial meals of Moab and then in immorality with Moabite women, so that the shared table and the shared bed are one apostasy. The numbers differ between the accounts — Paul writes "three and twenty thousand" where Numbers records twenty-four thousand — a discrepancy readers have long noted and variously explained; his point rests on the event, not the tally.

crossRefs.label: Deuteronomy 32:16-17 — They sacrificed unto devils, not to God... They provoked him to jealousy
crossRefs.why: Both halves of Paul's argument are already here. The claim that pagan sacrifice terminates in devils rather than in the gods it names, and the response of divine jealousy that Paul invokes with "Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy?", are drawn from the Song of Moses. The allusion also carries its own context: this is the song given to Israel as a witness against them for the very failures Paul has just listed.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 24:1 — The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof
crossRefs.why: Paul quotes this twice in nine verses, and it does the liberating work in the chapter. If everything already belongs to God, then no pagan rite can transfer ownership of a piece of meat, and interrogating the butcher is unnecessary. The same psalm goes on to ask who may ascend the hill of the Lord and answers with clean hands and a pure heart, which is the balance Paul keeps: the creation is free to use, and the worshipper is still accountable.

crossRefs.label: John 6:51-56 — Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you
crossRefs.why: The discourse on the bread of life is the closest Gospel parallel to "the communion of the body of Christ," and it shares this chapter's framing: Jesus contrasts the manna Israel ate in the wilderness, after which "your fathers did eat manna... and are dead," with the bread that gives life. Paul makes the same comparison with the same conclusion, that the wilderness food did not save those who ate it, and both passages have long been the ground on which readings of the Eucharist are argued.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes the opening typology as a genuine sacramental parallel: the cloud and the sea prefigure baptism, the manna and the water from the rock prefigure the Eucharist, and Paul's whole warning depends on the correspondence being real. From this the tradition draws two conclusions it holds together. First, the sacraments truly give what they signify — the fathers really were "baptized unto Moses" and really did eat "spiritual meat," and Christ really was the Rock — so these are not bare emblems. Second, and just as strongly, the sacraments do not work as charms: those who received them all were nonetheless "overthrown in the wilderness," which is why the Church insists that a sacrament must be received with living faith and repentance, and why grave sin after baptism is a real danger requiring real remedy. The verse "let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall" is read as excluding presumption about one's own final salvation.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters agree that the passage is typological and that it is a warning against sacramental presumption — indeed many read it as the New Testament's sharpest argument against supposing that rites confer grace by their performance. The disagreement is over what conclusion follows. Reformed readings take the chapter as evidence that outward participation in the covenant community never guaranteed salvation, distinguishing the visible church from the elect and treating the wilderness generation as those who had the signs without the thing signified; the warning is genuine and is one means by which God preserves His own. Memorialist readings go further and take the parallel to show that the ordinances are signs of a grace already received by faith, not channels of it. Those Protestants who hold that grace can be finally lost read the passage much as Catholics do. All agree that Paul's practical instruction is identical on either account: "flee from idolatry."

interpretationNotes.claim: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" is, in Catholic reading, among the plainest New Testament statements of the real presence. The argument turns on it: Paul is explaining why one cannot eat at a shrine, and the explanation only works if eating at the Lord's table joins the communicant to Christ as objectively as eating at a pagan table joins the eater to what is sacrificed there. The words are read at face value — what is shared is the blood and the body, not a symbol of them — and the phrase "which we bless" is understood to name an action performed over the cup, a consecration by the Church, rather than mere thanksgiving before a meal. The next verse then draws the ecclesial consequence: "we being many are one bread, and one body," so that the sacrament both presupposes and creates the unity of the Church.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings range widely and the range matters. Sacramental Protestants hold that Christ is truly given and received in the Supper, so that the participation Paul describes is real communion with the crucified Christ, while declining the account of how the elements are changed. Reformed readings emphasize that the word rendered "communion" means sharing or participation, and that believers are genuinely made partakers of Christ by the Spirit in the act of receiving, though the body remains where the ascended Christ is; the sharing is real and spiritual rather than local. Memorialist readings take the participation to be fellowship in the benefits of Christ's death and in the body of believers, pointing to the next verse's "one bread, and one body" as evidence that Paul's concern is corporate belonging. All these readings agree with the Catholic one on the argument's structure: the Supper creates a binding allegiance, which is exactly why it cannot be combined with the table of devils.

interpretationNotes.claim: In Catholic reading, the three-way comparison Paul draws — the Lord's table, Israel's altar, and "the table of devils" — implies that the Christian table is itself an altar and that what happens there is sacrificial. Paul asks, "Behold Israel after the flesh: are not they which eat of the sacrifices partakers of the altar?" and applies the same category on both sides of it; the middle term of the comparison is sacrifice, and a comparison between two sacrificial meals and a merely commemorative one would break down. On this reading the Eucharist is the making-present of the one sacrifice of Calvary rather than a new or additional offering, which is why the Church can call it a sacrifice without implying that Christ suffers again, and why the language of altar, table, and partaking sits together naturally in this passage.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters answer that Paul's point of comparison is not sacrifice but fellowship and allegiance. What the three tables share is that eating at any of them declares whose you are and binds you to that company; the argument works on that basis alone and does not require the Supper to be an offering. They urge that the New Testament writers avoid calling the Christian assembly's table an altar in the sacrificial sense, and that the letter to the Hebrews insists on a single offering made once and never repeated, so that a continuing sacrifice would obscure the finished work it proclaims. In their reading the Supper shows forth a sacrifice rather than performing one. Both traditions affirm that the death of Christ is unrepeatable and sufficient, that the Supper is inseparably tied to it, and that partaking makes a public declaration of allegiance that cannot be doubled.

authoring.attributionNotes: Original synthesis grounded in the KJV text and the general Catholic/Christian interpretive tradition. No specific published source is quoted or cited; tradition labels denote a position, not a copied source.
